::: callout-note
## Biological question

In the same growth chamber, some wild *Arabidopsis* plants flower after 6 weeks, others
after 4 months. Which regions of their genome explain the difference, and how do we
avoid being fooled by where the plants come from?
:::

In Session 4 you ran **one** linear model. In Session 5 you ran one test per molecule,
34 then 2,500 tests, and corrected the p-values. Today you run **more than 20,000 linear
models**, one per position of the genome where the plants differ: a **genome-wide association
study** (GWAS). The data are real and public: about 1,000 wild lines of *Arabidopsis
thaliana* collected across Europe and Asia, sequenced by the 1001 Genomes project, and
grown side by side to measure when they flower.

You will see that the naive analysis finds "significant" positions everywhere, and why:
plants from the same region share both their DNA and their flowering behaviour. The PCA
of Session 5, run on the DNA, finds this **population structure** and lets you correct
for it. What remains points to a famous flowering gene. Then you do the same alone on a
second trait, the sodium in the leaves, where the story is different.

### Learning outcomes

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- explain what a SNP is, and how a genotype table is coded (0/1);
- test one SNP with the linear model of Session 4, then all SNPs with a function and
  `apply()`;
- explain why thousands of tests need a stricter threshold (Bonferroni), and draw a
  Manhattan plot;
- read a QQ plot and the inflation factor λ, and say when a scan cannot be trusted;
- explain how population structure creates false associations, find it with a PCA of
  the genotypes, and correct for it with principal components as covariates;
- go from a peak to a list of candidate genes, and say what a GWAS can and cannot prove.

## Theory (≈45 min)

### 1. The question: natural variation

Individuals of one species differ, and part of these differences is written in their
DNA. A **GWAS** asks: *at which positions of the genome do the individuals with a high
value of a trait tend to carry a different letter than those with a low value?*

***Arabidopsis thaliana*** is ideal for this. It fertilises itself, so a wild line, an
**accession**, is almost completely homozygous: its seeds are genetically identical to
the parent plant. An accession can be sequenced once and grown as many times as needed,
in as many conditions as needed. The **1001 Genomes** project (2016) sequenced 1,135
accessions and found about 10 million positions where they differ.

### 2. The data: SNPs coded 0 and 1

A **SNP** (single nucleotide polymorphism) is one position of the genome where some
accessions carry one letter and others another, for example `A` or `G`. Today's genotype
table keeps more than 20,000 SNPs, about one every 5,000 bases, coded:

- **0**: the accession has the same letter as the reference genome (the lab accession
  Col-0);
- **1**: it has the other letter.

0 does not mean "normal" and 1 does not mean "mutant": 0 only means "like Col-0". Each
accession is homozygous, so there are only two values (in humans, who carry two
different copies, the coding is 0, 1 or 2).

Only SNPs whose rarer letter is carried by at least 5% of the accessions were kept (the
**minor allele frequency**, MAF ≥ 5%): a letter carried by 3 plants out of 1,000 would be
tested on 3 plants only, and one odd plant would be enough to make it look important.

The table has one row per SNP, as in the VCF format used in genomics, and one column per
accession. In R, you turn it into a **matrix** of 0 and 1, as you did with the
metabolites in Session 5.

### 3. One linear model per SNP

For one SNP, the question is the one of Session 4: does the flowering time differ between
the plants with allele 0 and those with allele 1?

```r
lm(flowering ~ allele)
```

The `Estimate` of `allele` is the difference between the two means, in days; its p-value
says whether the difference is larger than chance. A GWAS repeats this model for every
SNP and keeps the p-values: thousands of models, each a fraction of a second.

**Many tests.** At the 5% level, 1 test in 20 is "significant" by chance alone: with
thousands of SNPs, that makes hundreds of false positives, even if no SNP did anything. GWAS use the
**Bonferroni** threshold: 5% divided by the number of tests. Only SNPs below it are
called significant. It is stricter than the FDR correction of Session 5 (it controls the
risk of even one false positive in the whole genome), and it is the usual choice in
GWAS.

**The Manhattan plot** shows all the tests at once: the position of each SNP along the
five chromosomes on the x axis, −log10(p) on the y axis (p = 0.01 becomes 2, 10⁻⁶
becomes 6: high means strong evidence), and a line at the Bonferroni threshold. A real
association looks like a **tower**: not one point, but several neighbouring SNPs raised
together, because neighbouring SNPs are inherited together (**linkage
disequilibrium**).

### 4. Can the scan be trusted? The QQ plot

If no SNP had any effect, the p-values would be spread evenly between 0 and 1. The **QQ
plot** compares the observed p-values (sorted) with these expected ones, both on the
−log10 scale:

- points on the diagonal, with a few rising at the top right only: a healthy scan, with
  a few real associations;
- the whole curve above the diagonal, almost from the start: too many small p-values
  **everywhere**, a sign of a hidden problem.

The **inflation factor λ** sums up the QQ plot in one number: λ = 1 means no inflation;
above about 1.1, be suspicious. It is computed from the median SNP, so a few real peaks
do not change it.

### 5. The confounder: population structure

Plants from the same region share ancestry: over most of the genome, two Swedish
accessions are more alike than a Swedish and a Spanish one. Thousands of letters are
therefore frequent in Sweden and rare elsewhere, for purely historical reasons. If the
trait **also** differs between regions (say, if the plants of one region flower late),
then every SNP with a letter typical of that region looks associated with late
flowering. The SNP did nothing: it
only tells where the plant comes from. Ancestry is a **confounder**, like a place on the
bench could have been one in the soybean experiment of Session 4, if the plants had not
been randomised. In nature, nothing is randomised.

**The fix.** The PCA of Session 5, run on the genotype matrix (accessions in rows, SNPs
in columns), finds the main axes of genetic differences between accessions: they follow
ancestry, and geography. Adding the first principal components to every model,

```r
lm(flowering ~ allele + pcs)
```

changes the question to: *among accessions of similar ancestry, do those with allele 1
flower later?* This is what adding `heat` next to `water` did in Session 4: an effect
"adjusted for" another variable. Professionals go one step further with **mixed models**
and a kinship matrix (the genetic similarity of every pair of plants); we stay with the
PCs, which you already know.

### 6. From a peak to a gene

The best SNP of a tower is a **marker**, not necessarily the cause: it travels with the
real cause, which may be another SNP, a deletion, or anything nearby. In
*Arabidopsis*, this travelling together usually fades within about 10,000 bases, so you
list the genes within ±20 kb of the best SNP, read what they do, and choose the most
plausible one. Databases help: [TAIR](https://www.arabidopsis.org) for *Arabidopsis*
genes, [UniProt](https://www.uniprot.org) for proteins (Session 3). A GWAS gives
**candidates**; only experiments (mutants, swapping alleles between plants) prove that a
gene causes the difference.

**Which plot, for which question?**

| Your question | Plot or number | In R |
|---|---|---|
| Does one SNP change the trait, and by how much? | boxplot by allele, linear model | `geom_boxplot()`, `lm()` |
| Where in the genome are the associations? | Manhattan plot | `geom_point()` + `facet_grid()` |
| Can I trust the scan as a whole? | QQ plot, λ | `ppoints()`, `qchisq()` |
| Do the plants differ by ancestry? | PCA of the genotypes | `prcomp()` |
| Which genes sit under a peak? | the gene table, ±20 kb | `filter()` |

### 7. Worked example: the 1001 Genomes plants

- **Flowering time** (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016): each accession was grown in growth
  chambers at a constant **10 °C** or **16 °C**, 16 hours of light, **without any
  winter**, 4 plants per accession. The trait is the number of days from sowing to the
  first open flower (the mean of the 4 plants).
- **Leaf sodium** (Baxter et al., 2010): plants of about 150 of these accessions were grown in
  the same soil, and the sodium in their leaves measured by mass spectrometry. Too much
  sodium is toxic for plants: it is the main problem of salty soils.
- **Genetic groups**: the 1001 Genomes project grouped the accessions by ancestry
  (`north_sweden`, `spain`, `relict`, ...); accessions with mixed ancestry are `admixed`.
  You will use these groups only to look at the results, never in the GWAS itself.

### Practical briefing

Blocks A-E in pairs, block F on your own. Block B meets the plants without any
statistics: where they come from, and when they flower. Block C tests two SNPs by hand:
one that does nothing, and one that looks important but lies. Block D tests all the
SNPs, flowering at 16 °C; block E finds the structure with a PCA, corrects the GWAS, and
looks up the gene under the best peak. Block F does the same alone for leaf sodium: same

## Your R toolbox

New tools today, on top of the Session 4 and Session 5 toolboxes (still valid: see the
[Session 4 R toolbox](04_biological_tables_and_visualisation.qmd#your-r-toolbox)).

::: panel-tabset
## A function and apply()

A **function** packs a few lines of code under a name, so that you can run them again
on other data:

```r
snp_p_value <- function(allele) {
  fit <- lm(flowering ~ allele)
  summary(fit)$coefficients["allele", "Pr(>|t|)"]
}
```

- `allele` is the **argument**: the data you give the function each time you call it;
- the last line is what the function returns: here the p-value of the row `allele` in
  the table of coefficients of `summary(fit)`;
- `flowering` is not an argument: the function finds it in your session, so create it
  first.

`apply()` runs a function on every row (or column) of a matrix:

```r
apply(genotype_matrix, 1, snp_p_value)   # 1 = each row, 2 = each column
```

It returns one value per row: here one p-value per SNP, in the order of the rows.

**Common mistake.** `object 'flowering' not found`: run the line that creates
`flowering` before `apply()`.

## Matrices: rows, columns, t()

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `genotype_matrix["chr1_920099", ]` | one row (one SNP), all columns (all accessions) |
| `genotype_matrix[, 1:5]` | all rows, the first 5 columns |
| `dim(genotype_matrix)` | number of rows, then of columns |
| `t(genotype_matrix)` | turns the matrix around: rows become columns |
| `rownames()`, `colnames()` | the names of the rows and of the columns |

`prcomp()` wants the samples (here the accessions) in rows, hence `t()`.

## Manhattan plot

```r
ggplot(gwas, aes(x = position / 1e6, y = -log10(p_value))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(threshold), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(~ chromosome, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x")
```

- `position / 1e6`: positions in millions of bases (Mb);
- `facet_grid(~ chromosome, ...)`: one panel per chromosome, side by side;
  `scales = "free_x"` gives each panel its own x axis, `space = "free_x"` makes each
  panel as wide as its chromosome is long.

## QQ plot and λ

```r
qq <- gwas %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  mutate(expected = -log10(ppoints(n())),
         observed = -log10(p_value))
```

- `ppoints(n())` gives `n` values spread evenly between 0 and 1: the p-values you would
  expect if no SNP had any effect;
- `geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1)` draws the diagonal.

The inflation factor:

```r
median(qchisq(p_values, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) / qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
```

`qchisq()` turns each p-value back into the test statistic it came from; λ compares the
median statistic with the one expected under "no effect".

## A map

```r
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "grey90", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = accessions, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-12, 90), ylim = c(30, 68))
```

- `map_data("world")` gives the outlines of the countries (from the package maps);
- `group = group` draws each country as its own shape;
- `coord_quickmap()` keeps the proportions of a map, and `xlim`/`ylim` zoom in.
:::

```r
one_snp %>% count(___)

  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Allele at chr1_920099", y = "Days to flowering at 16 °C")

summary(lm(flowering_16C ~ ___, data = one_snp))
```

### D. Guided: one linear model per SNP (16:10-16:35, pairs)

**D1. All the SNPs.** The model of C2, packed into a function, then run on every row of
the matrix:

```r
# the trait, in the same order as the columns of genotype_matrix
flowering <- accessions$flowering_16C

# the p-value of one SNP: the lm() of C2, written as a small function
snp_p_value <- function(allele) {
  fit <- lm(flowering ~ allele)
  summary(fit)$coefficients["allele", "Pr(>|t|)"]
}

# check it on the SNP of C3: the same p-value as there?
snp_p_value(genotype_matrix[___, ])

# now every SNP: apply() runs the function on each row (1) of the matrix (about 20 s)
p_naive <- apply(genotype_matrix, ___, snp_p_value)

# one row per SNP: its position and its p-value
gwas_naive <- genotypes %>%
  select(snp_id, chromosome, position) %>%
  mutate(p_value = ___)

gwas_naive %>% arrange(p_value)

# how many p-values below 0.05?
sum(gwas_naive$p_value < ___)
```

::: callout-note
## Checkpoint

The first line prints one p-value; `apply()` then works for about 20 seconds; the table
`gwas_naive` has 4 columns (`snp_id`, `chromosome`, `position`, `p_value`) and one row
per SNP. `object 'flowering' not found` means that the first line was not run.
:::

**D2. The threshold and the Manhattan plot.**

```r
# Bonferroni: 5% divided by the number of tests
threshold <- 0.05 / ___
threshold
-log10(threshold)
sum(gwas_naive$p_value < ___)

# the Manhattan plot: one point per SNP, one panel per chromosome
ggplot(gwas_naive, aes(x = position / 1e6, y = -log10(___))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(threshold), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_grid(~ chromosome, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Flowering at 16 °C, naive GWAS", x = "Position (Mb)", y = "-log10(p)")
```

**D3. The QQ plot and λ.**

```r
# expected: the p-values if no SNP had any effect (spread evenly between 0 and 1)
qq_naive <- gwas_naive %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  mutate(expected = -log10(ppoints(n())),
         observed = -log10(___))

ggplot(qq_naive, aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "QQ plot, naive GWAS", x = "Expected -log10(p)", y = "Observed -log10(p)")

# the inflation factor lambda: 1 means no inflation
lambda_naive <- median(qchisq(gwas_naive$p_value, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) /
  qchisq(0.5, df = 1)
lambda_naive
```

::: callout-note

### E. Guided: the population structure, then the corrected GWAS (16:35-17:10, pairs)

**E1. The PCA of the genotypes.** The same `prcomp()` as in Session 5, on all the
accessions and all the SNPs (about 30 seconds):

```r
# the PCA of Session 5: accessions in rows (t() turns the matrix), SNPs in columns (about 30 s)
genotype_pca <- prcomp(t(___), scale. = ___)

pca_variance <- round(100 * summary(genotype_pca)$importance[2, 1:10], 1)
pca_variance

pca_scores <- as_tibble(genotype_pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(select(accessions, genetic_group, latitude, longitude))

ggplot(pca_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = ___)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", pca_variance[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", pca_variance[___], "%)"),
       colour = "Genetic group")

# does PC1 follow geography?
cor(pca_scores$PC1, pca_scores$___, use = "complete.obs")
cor(pca_scores$PC1, pca_scores$longitude, use = "complete.obs")
```

```r
sum(gwas_pc$p_value < ___)

# the Manhattan plot (as in D2)
```

```r
top_snp

         end > top_snp$position - ___,
         start < top_snp$position + 20000)

# the same SNP in the naive scan: its p-value, and how many SNPs had a smaller one
```

**E4, continued: the gene names on the plot.** Nothing to fill: after your answer to E4,
run this chunk. It draws the Manhattan plot of E3 again, with the best SNP in blue and
the short names of the genes within 20 kb of it.

```r
# the short names of the genes within 20 kb of the best SNP (the same genes as above)
top_genes <- genes %>%
  filter(chromosome == top_snp$chromosome,
         end > top_snp$position - 20000,
         start < top_snp$position + 20000,
         !is.na(symbol)) %>%
  mutate(symbol = str_replace_all(symbol, "%3B", ";"))   # the file writes ";" as %3B
top_label <- top_snp %>%
  mutate(genes = paste(top_genes$symbol, collapse = "\n"))   # one name per line

# the Manhattan plot of E3, with the best SNP in blue and the names of its genes
ggplot(gwas_pc, aes(x = position / 1e6, y = -log10(p_value))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(threshold), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(data = top_label, colour = "blue", size = 2) +
  geom_label(data = top_label, aes(label = genes), hjust = 0, vjust = 1, nudge_x = 1,
             size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(~ chromosome, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "The genes near the best SNP (10 PCs)",
       x = "Position (Mb)", y = "-log10(p)")
```

## Checkpoint

You are done when all of the following are true:

- you can say what a SNP is and what 0 and 1 mean in the genotype table;
- you tested one SNP with `lm()`, then all of them with a function and `apply()`;
- you can explain the Bonferroni threshold, and read a Manhattan plot;
- you can read a QQ plot and λ, and say when a scan cannot be trusted;
- you can explain, with the SNP of C3, how population structure creates false
  associations;
- you ran a PCA of the genotypes, and used its components to correct the GWAS;
- you found the genes under a peak, and can say why a peak is not a proof;
- you can explain why the structure misleads the GWAS of flowering time much more than
  that of leaf sodium.

## Going further

- Korte A. and Farlow A. (2013). [The advantages and limitations of trait analysis with
  GWAS: a review](https://doi.org/10.1186/1746-4811-9-29). *Plant Methods*. The best
  short review for plant biologists.
- 1001 Genomes Consortium (2016). [1,135 genomes reveal the global pattern of
  polymorphism in *Arabidopsis thaliana*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2016.05.063).
  *Cell*. Where today's SNPs and flowering times come from.
- [AraGWAS Catalog](https://aragwas.1001genomes.org): published *Arabidopsis* GWAS,
  including flowering time, run with mixed models: compare with your peaks.
- [AraPheno](https://arapheno.1001genomes.org): hundreds of other traits measured on the
  same accessions.
